abstract: We conduct an empirical examination to address the emerging hypothesis that label smoothing hinders knowledge distillation. First, we outline the rationale for this potential interference, specifically focusing on how label smoothing diminishes the relative knowledge within teacher logits. A framework is established for evaluating the impact of label smoothing on the distribution of classes categorized by semantic similarity. Furthermore, we define a quantitative metric to assess the extent of information loss within sample features. We then challenge the assumption that this incompatibility is universal, utilizing extensive experimental evaluations, visualizations, and broad analyses across Binary Networks, Image Classification, and Neural Machine Translation. The study concludes with a discussion regarding specific scenarios where label smoothing may negatively influence model performance.

author: Clark
title: Employing Knowledge Distillation for Agnostic Federated Learning Frameworks
abstract: Can we construct a generalized interface enabling decentralized entities to participate in collaborative model training without architectural restrictions? This system must operate without requiring identical network designs across participants or access to shared public datasets. Knowledge distillation serves as the primary mechanism for these collaborative approaches. Counterintuitively, we demonstrate that standard knowledge distillation strategies applied to federated learning yield subpar results. We introduce a formal mathematical model, Federated Kernel ridge regression, to examine the impacts of varying data distributions and distinct model architectures. Our findings reveal that inferior outcomes stem from intrinsic flaws in knowledge distillation when local training sets differ significantly. By applying this framework, we formulate and test alternative protocols utilizing knowledge distillation. Observed outcomes from neural network trials align with our analytical projections, confirming the persistent limitations of these techniques.

author: Hahn
title: Pearson Correlation Coefficient for Generalized Object Detector Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While knowledge distillation serves as a prevalent approach for producing lightweight object detectors, research into cross-architecture distillation remains insufficient. Our experimental analysis demonstrates that student models benefit from superior FPN features supplied by heterogeneous teacher detectors, notwithstanding disparities in label assignment strategies and detection heads. Nevertheless, naive feature map alignment encounters dual obstacles: feature intensity mismatches impose excessively rigid requirements on the student, and teacher FPN channels or stages with substantial magnitudes disproportionately influence distillation loss gradients, introducing noise while obscuring minor feature signals. To resolve these challenges, the proposed method utilizes the Pearson Correlation Coefficient to emulate teacher relational patterns, thereby decoupling magnitude dependencies. Empirical results indicate that this technique surpasses previous detection distillation strategies across both consistent and varied teacher-student pairings while exhibiting improved convergence rates. Utilizing a MaskRCNN-Swin teacher, ResNet-50 RetinaNet and FCOS architectures reach 41.5% and 43.9% mAP respectively on COCO2017, reflecting gains of 4.1% and 4.8% over standard baselines.

author: Walter
title: Optimizing Knowledge Distillation when Utilizing Highly Capable Teachers
abstract: While conventional knowledge distillation frameworks often prioritize standard configurations lacking cutting-edge teacher proficiency, this study introduces the proposed method for superior knowledge transfer from robust teachers. Our experimental observations indicate that pronounced divergence in output logits between a student and an elite teacher frequently disrupts the optimization process, rendering standard KL divergence-based alignment ineffective. Instead, our approach demonstrates that maintaining structural dependencies within output distributions is adequate, and we formulate a correlation-based loss to explicitly encode inherent inter-class relationships derived from the teacher. Furthermore, by accounting for varying semantic affinities across individual samples, we generalize this relational alignment to encompass intra-class dynamics. This methodology provides a straightforward yet effective solution, with comprehensive evaluations confirming that it accommodates diverse model architectures, capacity scales, and training paradigms, yielding consistent state-of-the-art accuracy across object detection, image classification, and semantic segmentation benchmarks. Source code is published at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Maintaining Data Confidentiality within Federated Learning through Aggregate Multi-Source Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) functions as an approach for distributed model training where nodes perform local computations without exposing their raw datasets. Traditional FL strategies commonly utilize parameter exchange or co-distillation to mitigate heterogeneity in data, yet these techniques encounter constraints related to communication overhead and potential privacy compromise. Here, we introduce a methodology for FL that maximizes communication efficiency and data protection by utilizing a singular offline knowledge distillation cycle involving public, cross-domain, unlabeled datasets. By implementing a quantized, noisy ensemble derived from fully optimized local model logits, our proposed method strengthens privacy safeguards while maintaining prediction performance. Our empirical evaluations across image and text classification benchmarks demonstrate that this approach surpasses standard FL algorithms regarding predictive accuracy and communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Modeling via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Large-scale text corpora are frequently analyzed through topic models to extract semantic patterns that humans can readily grasp. By leveraging knowledge distillation, this work synthesizes the optimal characteristics inherent in pretrained transformers and probabilistic topic models. This flexible approach facilitates seamless integration into any neural topic model to elevate topic quality, a capability validated across two models with distinct architectures that achieve peak levels of topic coherence. Beyond the typical reporting of average performance across all topics, our findings indicate that the proposed method also secures gains when examining aligned topics in direct side-by-side evaluations.

author: Foster
title: Optimizing Click-Through Rate Estimation via Aggregated Teacher Distillation
abstract: Deep learning architectures have gained prominence in click-through rate (CTR) prediction, delivering superior performance across diverse production environments. Yet, prevailing efforts prioritize intricate network designs to enhance the representation of complex feature relationships and evolving user patterns, potentially increasing latency and complicating real-time deployment. We shift focus toward a novel training paradigm centered on knowledge distillation (KD), a teacher-student framework facilitating the migration of learned insights from a primary model to a more efficient counterpart. This methodology enables the implementation of a streamlined student model based on a vanilla DNN while simultaneously surpassing the performance metrics of existing teacher models. Building upon these findings, we investigate the efficacy of employing an ensemble of teachers to refine student training. Our proposed method incorporates specialized techniques to support aggregated CTR estimation, specifically incorporating teacher gating mechanisms and monitoring distillation loss for early stopping. Rigorous evaluation across three industrial datasets against 12 baseline models confirms our approach. Both retrospective performance assessments and live A/B testing validate the performance gains achieved through this KD-based training framework.

author: Rocha
title: Utilizing Cross Distillation for Low-Data Neural Architecture Reduction
abstract: Reducing deep learning model complexity is a standard practice for generating efficient architectures. Nevertheless, typical techniques necessitate substantial datasets for post-compression adjustment, a requirement that frequently conflicts with data confidentiality and protective constraints. To balance data security with predictive capability, this work examines few shot network compression: how might we minimize a network's parameter count using minimal samples per category without incurring significant accuracy losses? A primary obstacle here is that the student model easily exhibits overfitting to the limited data, which exacerbates estimation errors originating from the teacher network during prediction. These inaccuracies tend to aggregate across successive layers, ultimately undermining final outputs. We mitigate this by introducing the proposed method, a technique involving layer-wise knowledge distillation. By alternating the hidden layers of the student and the teacher, we successfully suppress the buildup of layer-specific estimation errors. This strategy provides a versatile mechanism that integrates seamlessly with existing compression protocols like pruning. Comprehensive testing on standard benchmarks verifies that the proposed method substantially boosts student network accuracy in regimes constrained to few training instances.

author: Ellis
title: Investigating Embedding-Based Model Compression Techniques for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: The distillation of knowledge serves as a methodology for improving the efficiency of lightweight GNNs by leveraging the predictive power of complex teacher models. Previous research introduced the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), a technique that enforces correspondence in edge-based local topological configurations between teacher and student node features. We examine if forcing the student to replicate the teacher's global embedding topology offers a superior objective, particularly given that practical graphs frequently exhibit ambiguous edges and hidden dependencies. The proposed method utilizes contrastive learning to enforce global topological alignment by mapping student features to teacher representations within a unified vector space. Furthermore, we present an increased collection of large-scale benchmark datasets, specifically chosen for their substantial performance disparity between teacher and student GNN architectures. Evaluations conducted on 14 diverse GNN models across 4 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method reliably enhances the accuracy and stability of efficient GNNs, surpassing LSP, its global structure-preserving variation, and established methods adapted from 2D computer vision. Examination of the similarity between embedding spaces suggests that the proposed method effectively manages both local and global relational constraints, whereas existing structure-focused techniques tend to prioritize one at the expense of the other. The implementation is provided at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Enhancing Rare Token Performance: Optimizing Dual Data Sources for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) systems often utilizes knowledge distillation (KD) to generate synthetic training sets. Unfortunately, a mismatch regarding rare tokens between authentic and distilled samples increases predictive inaccuracies for these specific entries. Pretraining NAT architectures with raw data addresses this issue. Investigative mapping reveals that KD enforces deterministic alignment from source rare tokens to targets yet provides insufficient reverse mapping. Therefore, we introduce reverse KD to recover additional alignments for infrequent target tokens. Integrating these mutually beneficial techniques creates a novel training methodology to enhance NAT efficacy. Evaluations spanning five datasets and two state-of-the-art frameworks confirm that this technique provides universal quality gains by lowering rare token prediction failures. This strategy yields 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU scores on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English benchmarks. All resources are published at https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT.

author: Wright
title: Knowledge Transfer for Holistic Video-Based Environment Perception
abstract: Attaining complete environmental awareness remains essential for automated platforms. Studies indicate that deep neural networks are capable of acquiring geometric depth and optical flow kinematics from single-view video streams absent human-provided labeling, which remains difficult to acquire for these dual objectives. This research advances integrated scene perception through single cameras by training for depth, movement, and semantic labels concurrently, utilizing a pre-trained model to distill surrogate ground truth. Our approach incorporates these three goals via 1) an original learning strategy utilizing knowledge distillation combined with self-supervision and 2) a lightweight network structure that facilitates rapid scene parsing on both resource-intensive graphical processors and energy-constrained edge hardware. Empirical validation demonstrates that our proposed method achieves top-tier metrics regarding monocular depth, optical flow, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Collaborative Model Output Transfer
abstract: Rather than exposing sensitive raw datasets, decentralized training architectures typically transmit internal parameters between nodes. The standard federated learning approach transmits neural network weights or gradients, but these transmissions prove prohibitively expensive given constrained bandwidth, especially for contemporary deep neural networks characterized by massive parameter counts. As a viable alternative, the proposed method utilizes knowledge distillation to transmit only model logits, which possess significantly lower dimensionality than the full model architectures, such as the 10-class output space of MNIST. This text examines the proposed method to clarify its operational utility and efficiency in communication across diverse scenarios. Initially, the mechanism is explored through asymptotic analysis applied to the two base paradigms of knowledge distillation and co-distillation, utilizing neural tangent kernel theory. Following this, the performance of the proposed method in classification tasks is benchmarked against standard federated learning protocols, assessing both predictive accuracy and transmission requirements. The final section validates the flexibility of the proposed method through two specific implementations: reinforcement learning scenarios and asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless network environments.

author: Baker
title: Synthesizing Distinctive Models via Distillation
abstract: We examine the challenge of merging intelligence from various classifiers, characterized by distinct architectures and disparate target classes, into one student model using solely unlabeled instances. This scenario emerges when information originates from multiple providers restricted from disclosing raw data—for instance, because of confidentiality constraints—limiting sharing to the student teacher models themselves. Furthermore, inconsistent data accessibility at each site prevents uniform class coverage, while hardware variations lead to differing model capacities. To address this, we introduce a broadened approach to distillation for consolidating these disparate systems. A mathematical connection is established relating teacher logits to the overarching class probability distribution. Leveraging this framework, we formulate two strategies relying on cross-entropy loss reduction and matrix factorisation, enabling the approximation of soft labels across all categories from unlabeled inputs to facilitate training the unified student. Rigorous evaluations on Places365, LSUN, and ImageNet demonstrate that our proposed method beats basic distillation variants and approaches the performance of models developed through centralized, fully supervised training.

author: Richards
title: Utilizing Knowledge Distillation and Generative Adversarial Networks for Linguistic Synthesis
abstract: Within NLP domains like text summarization, language modeling, and machine translation, producing natural language remains a central objective. While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have attained significant milestones regarding image fidelity, applying these frameworks to natural language is hindered by the non-continuous attributes of text. This paper details a strategy leveraging knowledge distillation to facilitate GAN training for generating text. We illustrate the utility of autoencoders (AEs) to generate continuous sentence features, characterized by smooth probability distributions across multiple vocabulary tokens. By distilling these feature spaces, our generator learns to produce analogous smooth representations. Empirical evaluations across diverse datasets confirm that the proposed method outperforms conventional GAN-based architectures that lack pre-training, as evidenced by improved Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) metrics and higher BLEU score results.

author: Hurst
title: Optimizing Ranking Model Efficiency Through Distillation for Recommendation Engines
abstract: We introduce a fresh approach for constructing ranking systems that balance high performance with computational lightness. Given the established efficacy of knowledge distillation (KD) in computer vision for improving speed and accuracy, we implement a KD strategy tailored for ranking tasks, designated as the proposed method. Within this framework, a lightweight student model is optimized to order items by utilizing original training labels alongside guidance from an expansive teacher model. While maintaining comparable ranking accuracy to the heavier teacher, the student model significantly accelerates online inference due to its reduced parameter count. This technique is highly adaptable, functioning independently of the specific architectures selected for either the student or the teacher. We resolve several technical hurdles inherent to applying the proposed method in a ranking context. Evaluations conducted on standard benchmarks using top-tier recommendation architectures demonstrate that the proposed method meets its objectives; student models trained via this approach occupy less than 50% of the teacher's memory footprint while replicating its ranking quality, a marked improvement over student models trained in isolation.

author: Ross
title: Applying Collective Knowledge Transfer to Neural Machine Translation
abstract: The distillation of knowledge entails a procedure where a student model enhances its performance by emulating a superior teacher network. Because generating translations via an NMT engine demands significant latency, compact models serve to accelerate operational throughput. We illustrate the migration of output proficiency from both an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into one solitary NMT structure. Additionally, performance gains are realized when utilizing a teacher network that shares identical architecture and scale with the student network. Since training the student model remains computationally intensive, we employ a data filtering technique utilizing teacher-derived insights, which concurrently accelerates the learning phase and improves translation fidelity. Our methodology requires no architectural modification and integrates seamlessly with any NMT design to facilitate faster decoding.

author: Robinson
title: Enhancing Lexical Precision in Non-Autoregressive Translation Systems
abstract: The utilization of knowledge distillation (KD) remains vital for developing non-autoregressive translation (NAT) architectures, as it minimizes raw dataset difficulty through an autoregressive teacher model. This research provides empirical evidence that such training inadvertently transfers teacher-originated lexical choice inaccuracies for low-frequency words into the NAT model. To mitigate this, the proposed method incorporates raw training data to recover critical low-frequency word information otherwise absent in distilled sets. Specifically, we implement an auxiliary Kullback-Leibler divergence penalty that measures discrepancies between NAT model lexical selections and ground-truth raw data distributions. Tests across varied language pairs and model architectures verify the universal efficacy of this technique. Comprehensive investigations corroborate that the proposed method boosts quality by mitigating lexical choice errors affecting infrequent words. Notably, this framework advances SOTA NAT benchmarks to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU scores on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets. Code will be made available publicly.

author: Bright
title: Advancing Real-World Lipreading via Compact Distilled Architectures
abstract: The revival of neural networks has catalyzed substantial advancements in lipreading. While contemporary research prioritizes refined architectures and enhanced generalization capabilities, a notable disparity persists between existing techniques and the demands of field-ready deployment. This paper introduces several improvements to narrow this divide: initially, self-distillation is utilized to elevate benchmarks on LRW and LRW-1000, establishing new top scores of 88.5% and 46.6%. Furthermore, we introduce structural modifications, featuring a Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network head, which substantially minimizes floating-point operations compared to the baseline. We also demonstrate that knowledge distillation serves as a potent mechanism for restoring the accuracy of optimized, lightweight networks. This approach yields a spectrum of models balancing speed and precision. Notably, our primary low-latency models match previous top-tier results while achieving 8.2x lower computational complexity and 3.9x fewer parameters, facilitating the transition of lipreading systems into functional, real-world utility.

author: Hicks
title: Transferring Expertise: A Learning-based Adaptation Strategy
abstract: When training and testing distributions diverge, domain adaptation becomes a necessity for practical systems. Conventional Deep Learning frameworks for domain adaptation mandate simultaneous optimization over source and target sets, rendering them suboptimal for shifting domains or environments requiring frequent updates, such as adaptive spam filtering. Addressing these limitations, the proposed method adapts Knowledge Distillation principles for the domain adaptation task. Through leveraging domain-specific insights from various teachers and their inter-domain correlations, the student model attains superior unsupervised domain adaptation results on common sentiment benchmarks. Because assessing teacher reliability via simple domain similarity proves insufficient for single-source cases, the proposed method introduces a new metric to predict teacher performance within target domains. By integrating highly reliable instances identified through this metric, the student model reaches performance levels exceeding current standards for single-source adaptation.

author: Williams
title: Adversarial Belief Alignment for Data-Free Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The migration of information from a massive teacher model to a compact student architecture represents a prevalent objective within contemporary neural network deployments. Given the escalation of training set volumes combined with more stringent confidentiality mandates, the inability to reach the original training corpus is frequently encountered. This research introduces a framework for optimizing a student to emulate teacher logits absent any source data or auxiliary metadata. The approach utilizes an adversarial generator that identifies input patterns where the student deviates from the teacher, subsequently deploying these samples to refine student features and layers. For benchmarks such as SVHN, the student provides a near-identical mapping of the teacher, while on CIFAR10, the performance exceeds existing few-shot distillation benchmarks (utilizing 100 images per class) despite relying on zero training data. Furthermore, we define a measurement to assess belief matching congruence between networks near their respective decision boundaries, demonstrating that our zero-shot student achieves superior alignment to the teacher when compared against baselines distilled via actual data.

author: Rodriguez
title: Enhancing Performance via Knowledge Distillation: A Novel Approach to Surpassing Graph Neural Networks
abstract: The challenge of semi-supervised graph learning remains central to machine learning research. Current leading classification techniques utilize graph neural networks (GNNs), consistently eclipsing legacy approaches like label propagation. Yet, the intricate construction of these models often results in opaque inferential processes, failing to fully leverage intrinsic data patterns, such as the tendency for structurally linked nodes to share identical labels. To resolve this, we introduce a knowledge distillation framework. This technique captures information from any pre-trained GNN teacher model and transfers it into a streamlined student model. Our student architecture integrates feature transformation and label propagation, effectively capturing both attribute-based and structural-based prior knowledge. We specifically formulate the student as a trainable fusion of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation components. Consequently, the optimized student derives advantages from both inherent data priors and the distilled insights of GNN teachers to enhance predictive accuracy. Additionally, this student model provides a clearer, more interpretable inferential mechanism compared to GNNs. Evaluations across five benchmark datasets using seven GNN teachers, specifically GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP, demonstrate that the student model consistently exceeds the performance of its teacher by margins of 1.4% to 4.7% on average.

author: Burton
title: Optimizing Massive Language Representations via Block-Structured Pruning Designed for Hardware
abstract: While extensive pre-trained language models exhibit robust performance across various natural language processing domains, their adoption in edge computing environments is hindered by intensive computational requirements and substantial memory overhead. This paper introduces a technique to derive efficient transformer-based language representations utilizing hardware-aware block-structured pruning. By integrating reweighted group Lasso during the optimization process, the proposed method yields substantial improvements in compression ratios alongside marked reductions in parameter footprint and floating-point operations. Evaluations using BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT on the GLUE benchmark suite indicate that the proposed method enables up to 5.0x compression while maintaining near-original task performance. Furthermore, this approach complements existing strategies like knowledge distillation; applying it to DistilBERT yields an additional average 1.79x improvement in compression with negligible accuracy loss. Consequently, this methodology facilitates the effective deployment of language models on devices with restricted resources.

author: Conner
title: Transferring Targeted Insights from BERT to Compact Neural Architectures
abstract: Within the domain of natural language processing, a tendency exists toward constructing models of escalating depth and intricacy. Exemplars of this movement include GPT, ELMo, and the BERT language representation model. Such progress fosters a belief that earlier, less profound neural network designs possess no utility for linguistic comprehension. Contrary to this, we illustrate that basic, efficient neural networks remain potent contenders lacking any modifications to the structure, reliance on supplementary training resources, or the inclusion of extra input features. By applying distillation of knowledge from the high-performing BERT model into a solitary-layer BiLSTM and its associated siamese framework for dual-sentence operations, we bridge this gap. We observe performance parity with ELMo across an array of sentiment analysis, paraphrasing, and natural language inference tasks, while simultaneously reducing parameter count by a factor of 100 and cutting inference latency by 15 times.

author: Henderson
title: Enhancing Multi-Layer Perceptrons through Knowledge Distillation to Eliminate Graph Dependencies
abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve strong performance in node classification, their wide industrial adoption is hindered by scalability issues stemming from structural data dependency. Because GNN inference requires retrieving neighbor nodes across various hops, latency is significantly increased in real-time environments. While techniques like pruning and quantization decrease Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) counts, the fundamental bottleneck of data dependency remains, limiting overall gains. Alternatively, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) provide rapid inference without graph connectivity, though they typically exhibit inferior classification accuracy compared to GNNs. By leveraging knowledge distillation (KD) to unify these disparate approaches, we demonstrate that MLPs can achieve substantial performance gains. The proposed method enables inference without any reliance on an input graph. Our experiments reveal that the proposed method reaches competitive accuracy while achieving speedups of 146X-273X over GNNs and 14X-27X over alternative acceleration techniques. Across 7 datasets in both transductive and inductive scenarios, the proposed method increases accuracy by 12.36% on average versus independent MLPs and attains parity with GNNs in 6 out of 7 cases. Our results detail the conditions under which these models succeed, establishing the proposed method as an effective solution for low-latency requirements.

author: Brown
title: Integrated Methods for Reducing Vision Transformer Complexity
abstract: Vision transformers are increasingly favored for their strong benchmarks on large-scale datasets, despite lacking specialized convolution-based operations. Nevertheless, the heavy demands of multi-head self-attention mechanisms and other components result in substantial processing requirements. While convolutional neural networks have an extensive record of compression strategies, research into shrinking vision transformers is nascent, often targeting single objectives. We introduce an integrated methodology that consolidates pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. Our approach establishes a global, constrained optimization protocol to simultaneously determine model parameters, pruning masks, and layer skipping choices while minimizing a distillation loss. A primal-dual solver addresses this optimization task. Evaluations using ImageNet with DeiT and T2T-ViT architectures show that our technique yields superior results compared to recent baselines. Specifically, DeiT-Tiny attains a 50% reduction in FLOPs while preserving nearly all baseline accuracy. Open-source implementations are provided.

author: James
title: Advancing Cross-Modal Feature Encoding via Iterative Self-Distillation
abstract: The training paradigm of CLIP neglects the intricate, noisy many-to-many associations present in large-scale web-scraped visual-textual corpora, leading to suboptimal data utilization and computational overhead. We mitigate these issues by presenting a framework utilizing cross-modal contrastive training, leveraging progressive self-distillation and gradual image-text soft-alignments to attain improved feature robustness despite noisy inputs. The proposed method distills internal knowledge to construct dynamic soft-alignment labels for specific image-text pairs within each minibatch, subsequently guiding parameter refinement. Empirical testing on 14 benchmarks demonstrates that our approach surpasses CLIP performance in zero-shot classification, linear probe transfer, and image-text retrieval tasks, maintaining identical computational requirements. Investigations into ImageNet-derived robustness benchmarks indicate that our architecture achieves superior resilience against natural distribution variations than either ImageNet-specific models or CLIP. Finally, experiments across pretraining scales differing by a factor of 100 suggest that the performance gains over CLIP correlate positively with the total volume of training data.

author: Ferrell
title: Optimizing Supernet Learning via Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Automating the creation of neural architectures is efficiently addressed through weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS). In this approach, a supernet is constructed to incorporate every architecture as a sub-network, followed by simultaneous training of the supernet and these sub-networks. The efficacy of this paradigm depends significantly on the distillation of knowledge from the teacher supernet into the student sub-networks. Our investigation reveals that utilizing KL divergence for distillation often causes student sub-networks to miscalculate the uncertainty inherent in the teacher supernet, ultimately degrading performance. We introduce a strategy to refine supernet training by employing a generalized alpha-divergence. Choosing this metric adaptively permits us to mitigate inaccuracies regarding the teacher model's uncertainty. Our evaluation of this alpha-divergence methodology across slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS shows substantial gains. The resulting architectures surpass existing benchmarks such as BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS across diverse FLOPs ranges. We attained an ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% using 444M FLOPs. All implementations and pretrained weights are accessible via the provided repository.

author: Rice
title: Maintaining Representation in Sequential Fake Media Detection through Distillation
abstract: While AI development has surged, typical approaches remain shackled to static datasets and unchanging contexts. Continual learning offers an alternative framework where models process streams of connected data to emulate biological learning patterns. Concurrently, the rise of synthetic faces and deepfakes presents critical challenges for multimedia integrity. Although recent detectors achieve high precision, their performance degrades when constrained to static testing environments. We investigate integrating continual learning into neural network training to boost data efficiency. The proposed method synthesizes Representation Learning, Continual Learning, and Knowledge Distillation. By utilizing a teacher-student framework, the proposed method adapts sequentially to novel GAN-generated imagery and deepfake datasets while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Experimental evaluations verify that our technique excels at domain adaptation for recognizing poor-quality deepfakes and GAN outputs across various datasets, exceeding the performance of existing state-of-the-art baselines.

author: Maddox
title: Optimizing BERT Compression via Earth Mover's Distance and Many-to-Many Layer Alignment
abstract: While pre-trained language models such as BERT provide substantial utility across diverse natural language processing applications, their heavy memory and processing requirements impede efficient implementation on hardware with limited capacity. This study introduces an original BERT distillation technique utilizing many-to-many layer mapping, enabling every intermediate student layer to derive information from multiple teacher layers. Consequently, the proposed method adapts to distinct teacher layers based on specific natural language processing requirements. We utilize Earth Mover's Distance to determine the least total expense for transferring representations from the teacher network to the student network, facilitating robust many-to-many layer alignment. Moreover, we incorporate a cost attention mechanism to autonomously determine the layer weights for Earth Mover's Distance, which enhances predictive outcomes and quickens convergence. Comprehensive evaluations on the GLUE benchmark indicate that the proposed method reaches performance parity with leading techniques regarding both predictive precision and model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Systematic Review of Deep Learning Compression Techniques in Language Tasks
abstract: Advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) stem from deep learning architectures including RNNs, GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformer-based frameworks like BERT, GPT-2, MT-DNN, XLNet, T5, T-NLG, and GShard. These systems exhibit massive parameter counts, yet practical deployment necessitates minimized footprints, rapid inference, and reduced electrical demand. We analyze six distinct strategies—namely Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods—designed to compress these architectures for industrial NLP pipelines. Because of the vital requirement for lightweight models and the rapid growth of literature, this summary synthesizes recent contributions within the deep learning for NLP discipline into a structured narrative.

author: Smith
title: Automated Architecture Search for Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Mobile deployment needs for tasks like image editing, enhancement, and translation have recently increased interest in shrinking Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). While shrinking other deep architectures has seen significant activity, progress in condensing GANs—specifically generators—is presently limited. Current approaches to shrinking GANs often lack flexibility regarding loss functions and model architectures. By leveraging automated machine learning techniques, the proposed method addresses GAN condensation. By utilizing a custom-built, optimized search space, the proposed method discovers compact generators that satisfy prescribed computational budgets. These compressed models are derived through knowledge distillation guided by the source GAN. The proposed method operates autonomously, requires no discriminator training, and generalizes across diverse GAN architectures. Performance was assessed on super resolution and image translation benchmarks. The proposed method consistently produces compact models that surpass prior techniques in effectiveness. Resources are provided at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Enhancing Video-Pose representations for analyzing daily life movements
abstract: Efforts to fuse appearance data with 3D skeleton coordinates for identifying Activities of Daily Living (ADL) are prevalent. Since these activities frequently appear identical, capturing granular nuances is essential for differentiation. Due to the limited flexibility of current 3D ConvNets in detecting delicate temporal visual signals, current paradigms heavily rely on integrating RGB with 3D poses. However, deriving 3D poses from video signals incurs significant overhead without specialized hardware, hindering the deployment of these techniques in latency-sensitive environments. Consequently, what strategy maximizes the utility of 3D poses for ADL classification? We investigate two pathways for a pose-conditioned attention architecture: first, conveying pose-derived intelligence to RGB streams via feature-level distillation, and second, replicating pose-guided attention through attention-level distillation. A unified framework, the proposed method, combines these strategies. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method is performant, offers substantial acceleration, and maintains robustness against degraded pose quality. Across 4 benchmark datasets, the proposed method surpasses standard baselines regardless of the availability of 3D poses. Implementation details are accessible at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Feature-Based Knowledge Transfer via Imitation
abstract: The student-teacher paradigm represents a prevalent technique for optimizing lightweight models through the guidance of complex teachers. Conventional distillation practices rely on soft logits from the teacher as supplementary signals to guide student training. Our work posits that forcing the student to replicate features found in the penultimate layer yields superior results. Beyond capturing richer representations directly from teacher features, this imitation strategy functions even when teacher models lack a softmax layer. Empirical results demonstrate performance gains surpassing standard knowledge distillation. To optimize this imitation process, we analyze features by separating direction from magnitude. We contend that allowing flexibility in magnitude while prioritizing the alignment of feature directions improves outcomes. Accordingly, we introduce a loss function leveraging locality-sensitive hashing. This approach enhances the fidelity of direction matching, eases magnitude requirements, and establishes a new performance benchmark. We supply theoretical justifications for how locality-sensitive hashing assists in direction imitation and demonstrate the utility of this method across object detection and multi-label recognition tasks.

author: Herrera
title: Utilizing knowledge distillation for GAN parameter reduction
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are employed across diverse domains including synthetic data creation, super resolution, and style mapping. High-performing GANs frequently involve tens of millions of parameters, which creates significant overhead for real-time deployments or hardware constrained by low SWAP (size, weight, and power), like portable electronics. Existing literature lacks evidence of strategies to minimize parameter counts within GAN architectures. Consequently, we introduce a strategy for GAN compression through knowledge distillation, where a compact student GAN emulates the behavior of an expansive teacher GAN. Our results across Celeb-A, CIFAR-10, and MNIST demonstrate that the proposed method achieves compression ratios of 87:1, 58:1, and 1669:1 respectively, while preserving generated output fidelity. Our findings suggest a qualitative threshold for GAN compression. Additionally, given an identical parameter budget, we note that compressed GANs surpass performance levels of networks trained via traditional techniques. We hypothesize this is partly attributable to the optimization landscape inherent in over-parameterized GANs, facilitating effective learning via alternating gradient descent. Therefore, utilizing our proposed compression strategy subsequent to training an over-parameterized GAN yields a high-fidelity generative system with reduced parameter requirements.

author: Davidson
title: Enhancing Re-Identification Resilience through Multi-View Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While conventional Re-Identification approaches utilize tracking sequences in Video-To-Video paradigms to ensure stability, these models experience significant accuracy declines when applied to Image-To-Video search tasks. To mitigate this drop, recent literature focuses on distilling temporal features from video-centric models into image-centric architectures. We introduce a training procedure that enables the migration of high-quality insights derived from diverse angles of a subject. This proposed method utilizes visual diversity as a guiding signal inside a teacher-student schema, where a teacher instructs a student constrained to limited perspectives. Consequently, the student demonstrates superior efficacy compared to both the teacher and established benchmarks in Image-To-Video scenarios, yielding improvements of 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. Our comprehensive examination across animal, vehicular, and human Re-ID settings explores the characteristics of this technique through quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Implementation files are provided at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Deploying Graph Neural Networks Utilizing Differential Privacy Protections
abstract: Due to the rise in adoption of graph neural networks (GNNs) across confidential domains including medical fields, investigators have questioned the security of such models. Specifically, GNNs remain susceptible to membership inference attacks, which remain effective even given restricted black-box visibility to the model. We introduce a technique for the secure distribution of GNN architectures within centralized environments. By leveraging a publicly available unlabeled graph, the proposed method trains models on open data while incorporating insights derived from private datasets under strictly private conditions. This methodology integrates knowledge-distillation with random subsampling and noisy labeling to satisfy formal privacy bounds. The Renyi differential privacy framework facilitates our theoretical assessment of this design. Furthermore, empirical evaluations demonstrate the robust capability of our system against various alternative strategies tailored for graph-based information. Implementation resources are provided at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Hierarchical Auxiliary Regularization Applied to Federated Learning
abstract: The disparate nature and skewed distributions of client datasets impede federated learning, resulting in divergent local architectures and erratic global model convergence. To address these constraints, the proposed method implements an architectural regularization approach by integrating supplemental branches into every local network through the fusion of local and global subnetworks at diverse stages. The main pathway features are aligned with these auxiliary hybrid pathways through online knowledge distillation. This technique stabilizes the global model within non-iid environments, is compatible with diverse federated learning infrastructures, and necessitates zero additional communication overhead. Our exhaustive empirical evaluations indicate significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency over prior techniques.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation of Deep Neural Networks Without Access to Training Data
abstract: While contemporary compression strategies successfully reduce deep neural network parameter counts while maintaining near-original predictive performance, these techniques typically necessitate original training data availability. Such requirements prove prohibitive when dealing with expansive datasets or sensitive information, such as in biometric applications. We introduce a data-free knowledge distillation approach that enables the reduction of large-scale models using only supplemental metadata accompanying the pretrained network. We examine various metadata categories compatible with this framework and analyze the comparative performance implications of utilizing different types.

author: Mckay
title: Optimizing Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Model Efficiency
abstract: Massive language models achieve notable empirical outcomes, yet these advancements necessitate substantial parameter counts, increased energy usage, and higher latency, limiting deployment on restricted computational hardware. Knowledge distillation (KD) functions as a robust paradigm for model reduction. Nonetheless, deep architectures frequently exhibit overfitting to training samples, resulting in prediction instability during distribution shifts. Furthermore, insufficient task-specific training data restricts how effectively the student retrieves guidance from the teacher. To rectify these constraints, we introduce the proposed method, a data-independent distillation strategy utilizing mixup, an uncomplicated yet potent augmentation technique, to enhance the student's generalization. Specifically, the student replicates the teacher's logits not only on individual inputs but also on linear interpolations of input pairings. Theoretical analysis suggests that under standard assumptions, the proposed method reduces the disparity between empirical error and generalization error. Evaluations on the GLUE benchmark confirm that the proposed method yields consistent improvements over standard KD training and surpasses various state-of-the-art benchmarks. Assessments under data-scarce conditions and supplementary ablation analysis substantiate the benefits of this strategy.

author: Liu
title: Facilitating Multimodal Synthesis in CLIP Utilizing Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Advanced dual-stream architectures (for instance, CLIP) trained on massive image-text collections have demonstrated exceptional efficacy across alignment benchmarks. Nevertheless, these systems lack proficiency in multimodal generative domains because of the limited capacity of the text encoder. We address this limitation by integrating a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) into the dual-stream model using the proposed method of vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), which confers the necessary generative functionality. Compared to training ab initio, the proposed method is notably economical regarding computation and data requirements. Quantitative evaluations indicate robust zero-shot capabilities for generative objectives like image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. Specifically, the proposed method attains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on VQAv2, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art zero-shot benchmark while utilizing 7x fewer parameters. Moreover, since the PLM preserves its inherent aptitude for textual comprehension and generation post-VLKD, the architecture remains effective for both unimodal and multimodal applications.

author: Mason
title: Knowledge Transfer through Feature Embedding for Student Networks
abstract: While deep convolutional neural networks offer broad utility, their extensive memory and processing demands limit deployment on mobile hardware. Knowledge distillation improves lightweight student architectures by utilizing information from high-capacity teacher networks. Conventional distillation approaches frequently incorporate supplemental fully-connected layers to align teacher and student intermediate layers, resulting in significant overhead from extra parameters. Alternatively, the proposed method transfers teacher insights to the student without requiring the optimization of additional variables. We approach the teacher-student framework by framing it as a feature embedding task. By applying a locality preserving loss, the student is driven to produce low-dimensional features that capture the fundamental characteristics found within the teacher network's high-dimensional feature space. Consequently, this lightweight architecture preserves performance comparable to the teacher. We offer mathematical validation to confirm the reduced computational burden of the proposed method. Empirical evaluations on standard datasets and established networks indicate that the proposed algorithm surpasses current top-tier teacher-student learning techniques regarding efficiency in storage and computation.

author: White
title: Optimizing Lightweight Generative Adversarial Networks for Visual Synthesis
abstract: While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) effectively address diverse image-to-image translation objectives, their substantial memory requirements and computational demands hinder deployment on mobile hardware. Standard compression approaches typically target classification architectures rather than generation systems. Applying knowledge distillation, the proposed method trains a student generator with a reduced parameter count to acquire hierarchical feature representations from a bulky teacher generator. To enhance student generator efficacy, a student discriminator evaluates distributions between authentic images and synthetic outputs from both teacher and student models. This adversarial framework simultaneously refines the student generator and the student discriminator. Empirical benchmarks and visual assessments verify that the proposed method facilitates the creation of compact generative frameworks maintaining robust functionality.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Adaptive Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Widespread utility in diverse natural language processing benchmarks has been demonstrated by massive pre-trained language architectures like BERT. Deploying these models in resource-constrained environments necessitating rapid inference is hindered by their substantial parameter counts. Current approaches for distilling BERT into compact representations typically remain task-agnostic, applying identical compressed structures across disparate downstream objectives. To address the demand for specialized optimization, we introduce a proposed method that utilizes differentiable Neural Architecture Search for the automated generation of task-adaptive lightweight BERT variants. By integrating a task-specific knowledge distillation loss as a guidance mechanism alongside efficiency-conscious constraints, our approach achieves an optimal balance between performance and computational speed. Empirical validation across multiple NLP tasks reveals that these task-adaptive compressed models attain inference speeds 12.7x to 29.3x higher than original BERT, alongside a reduction in parameter volume of 11.5x to 17.0x, all while preserving comparable predictive accuracy.

author: Harrell
title: Ensuring Universal Participation: Federated Learning Across Diverse Computing Hardware
abstract: Federated learning (FL) serves as a critical strategy for developing unified models utilizing distributed data sets while maintaining privacy. Current FL frameworks frequently operate under the premise that every participant possesses the capacity to train the primary global model. Yet, actual deployments involve varied hardware, where clients exhibit disparate processing capabilities. While large-scale architectures like BERT demonstrate impressive artificial intelligence performance, implementing them within FL scenarios characterized by constrained clients presents significant hurdles. Naive approaches—such as excluding resource-limited participants or restricting the entire system to minimal models—generate drawbacks, specifically the marginalization of ignored clients or suboptimal precision stemming from truncated datasets or constrained model complexity. We introduce the proposed method, an inclusive FL strategy devised to address these limitations. The primary mechanism involves deploying model variants calibrated to specific device capacities, reserving larger architectures for high-performance nodes and compact versions for restricted ones. We further present a robust technique for synchronizing information across local models of varying scales, ensuring full participation across all clients to achieve a high-capacity global outcome. Furthermore, a momentum knowledge distillation procedure is utilized to refine information transfer from expansive models on robust hardware to streamlined variants on limited devices. Empirical evaluations conducted on multiple standard datasets verify the capability of the proposed method to train precise models within FL architectures containing heterogeneous client devices.

author: Evans
title: Optimizing Efficient Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: The field of machine translation and multilingual generation increasingly relies on regression-based evaluation metrics like BLEURT or COMET, which derive features from large multilingual architectures including mBERT or XLM-RoBERTa. However, research indicates that these architectures maximize effectiveness only at significant scales, creating substantial deployment overhead. By utilizing WMT Metrics Shared Task benchmarks, we examine the interplay between model capacity and multilingual proficiency within the RemBERT framework. Our analysis identifies model size as a primary constraint for cross-lingual transfer, which we mitigate via the proposed method. This technique utilizes synthetic data and distills knowledge from a single teacher into multiple students specialized in distinct language clusters. Consequently, the proposed method achieves a 10.5% gain compared to standard fine-tuning, retaining 92.6% of the original RemBERT performance while reducing parameter count by two-thirds.

author: Fowler
title: Visual Feature Learning via Self-supervised Distillation
abstract: We investigate methods for self-supervised learning applied to compact models. Data-driven observations indicate that prevalent contrastive self-supervised learning techniques achieve success for large architectures but perform inadequately when utilized for small models. To overcome this, we introduce the proposed method, which utilizes a massive network as a teacher to transmit its learned representations into a modest student architecture through a self-supervised process. Rather than relying on direct learning from raw data, our approach optimizes a student encoder to replicate the logit similarity distributions derived by a teacher across distinct instances. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method substantially enhances the capabilities of small-scale networks in downstream applications. Relative to existing self-supervised benchmarks, the proposed method increases top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k from 42.2% to 67.6% using EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% utilizing MobileNet-v3-Large.

author: Lynch
title: Transferring Knowledge Across Modalities for Action Recognition Using Vision-to-Sensor Distillation
abstract: The precision of human activity recognition (HAR) has been enhanced by recent multi-modal techniques. Nevertheless, these complex strategies are often incompatible with the limited processing power of wearable hardware like smartwatches. This work presents a proposed method for end-to-end knowledge distillation that bridges vision and sensor domains. By requiring only accelerometer time-series inputs for inference, the proposed method lessens the processing burden on edge hardware while maintaining accuracy comparable to resource-heavy multi-modal baselines. To preserve local temporal dynamics for visual deep learning architectures, we transform sensor streams into two-dimensional representations utilizing Gramian Angular Field (GAF) encoding. We utilize ResNet18 as the teacher and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as the student network. Furthermore, a proposed method employing a Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss function addresses modality disparities between vision and sensor signals. Validation across MMAct, UTD-MHAD, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets confirms the efficiency and performance of the proposed method for wearable sensor applications.

author: Hernandez
title: Transferring Knowledge from Neural Radiance Fields to Neural Light Fields for Accelerated View Synthesis
abstract: The surge in studies regarding Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) indicates promising capabilities for modeling intricate environments using deep learning. A primary limitation is the high computational cost of inference, as calculating one pixel necessitates querying the NeRF model hundreds of times. Current strategies primarily focus on minimizing sample point requirements, yet these approaches still rely on iterative marching. Conversely, Neural Light Field (NeLF) provides a simpler architecture for synthesizing novel views, where each pixel is produced in one forward pass, bypassing ray-marching altogether. We introduce a deep residual MLP architecture, comprising 88 layers, to capture the light field. Our findings suggest that high-capacity NeLF models necessitate abundant training data, which we obtain by distilling knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF. Our empirical evaluations across real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method versus competing techniques. On synthetic targets, we realize a 26-35x decrease in FLOPs per ray and a 28-31x acceleration in speed, while simultaneously attaining a superior image fidelity with 1.4-2.8 dB better PSNR compared to NeRF, all without requiring specialized parallel hardware.

author: Farmer
title: Streamlining 3D Object Detection via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Advanced 3D detectors encounter significant computational burdens regardless of significant advancements in the field. Consequently, we investigate knowledge distillation (KD) to foster high-efficiency 3D object detection, specifically examining voxel-based and pillar-based architectures. Lacking established teacher-student pairings, our initial efforts involve optimizing student accuracy-efficiency balances through input resolution scaling and model compression. Subsequently, we evaluate current 2D-centric KD techniques within the 3D domain using six curated teacher-student configurations. Moreover, we introduce an improved KD pipeline featuring an advanced logit KD approach; this method restricts distillation to critical locations identified by teacher classification logits, alongside teacher-guided initialization to migrate feature extraction capabilities through weight inheritance. Concluding testing on the Waymo dataset shows our leading model reaches 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, outperforming the teacher while utilizing merely 44% of its flops. Our fastest model attains 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, representing a 2.2x speedup over PointPillar while maintaining superior accuracy.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring information from multi-modal to mono-modal networks for segmentation tasks
abstract: In recent times, researchers have extensively examined combining diverse imaging modalities to segment medical images. Compared to mono-modal approaches, merging data across modalities typically enhances segmentation precision across numerous use cases. Nevertheless, clinical environments often preclude obtaining multiple modalities because of restricted scanning resources, time constraints, and budgetary limitations. Frequently, clinicians obtain just a single modality. This study introduces a methodology for distilling information from a pre-trained multi-modal teacher model into a mono-modal student model. Our approach modifies standard distillation techniques by instructing the student on a single modality input that represents a portion of the n-modal inputs utilized by the teacher. We validate this technique's efficacy for segmenting brain tumors using the BraTS 2018 dataset. Tests across various architectures indicate that the student effectively captures knowledge from the teacher, consistently achieving higher segmentation accuracy than the mono-modal baseline.

author: Osborne
title: Transferring Knowledge from Complex Models for Medical Informatics Use Cases
abstract: The rapid expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) presents fresh possibilities and pressing requirements for extracting significant evidence-based signatures and pathological trends within Computational Phenotyping studies. Although Deep Learning architectures demonstrate excellent efficacy for reliable forecasting in computational phenotyping, they possess challenges regarding model interpretability that remain vital for medical professionals during diagnostic choices. This work presents a new knowledge-distillation technique, the proposed method, which trains interpretable phenotype features to achieve dependable classification accuracy while emulating the predictive output of Deep Learning structures. Our architecture employs Gradient Boosting Trees to acquire transparent features derived from Deep Learning systems like Stacked Denoising Autoencoders and Long Short-Term Memory units. Rigorous testing using a practical clinical longitudinal dataset confirms that our approach achieves results comparable or superior to Deep Learning alternatives, while additionally supplying interpretable phenotypes to support clinical judgment.

author: Moreno
title: Agile Quadrotor Navigation Utilizing Perception-Integrated Control in Obstructed Spaces
abstract: Neural controllers have recently surpassed classical model-based planning schemes regarding rapid autonomous quadrotor transit within dense obstacles. Standard policies lack perception awareness, which is vital for vision-centric flight given quadrotor underactuation and constrained camera visibility. We present a machine learning framework enabling agile, perception-conscious maneuvering amidst clutter. This strategy integrates reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning through a privileged teacher-student paradigm. An RL-trained teacher policy initially learns time-optimal trajectories via full-state inputs. Subsequently, distillation via imitation learning transfers this expertise into a student policy restricted to visual sensor data. By fusing perception and control, this method yields a tenfold increase in computational efficiency alongside improved navigation success. Closed-loop control efficacy is validated through hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: Domain-Focused Optimization and Knowledge Transfer for Compact Pretrained Language Models
abstract: While extensive pretrained models excel across diverse language processing applications, their utility within specialized sectors is hindered by domain shift, complicating deployment due to throughput and memory limitations. We introduce a methodology for engineering lightweight, high-performance, domain-tailored pretrained models. Our framework integrates adaptation of existing general-purpose pretrained models with task-agnostic knowledge distillation conducted within target domains. In the adaptation phase, we implement domain-specific vocabulary augmentation, utilizing corpus-wide frequency metrics to autonomously determine incremental vocabulary scale. Furthermore, we evaluate varied techniques for compressing large pretrained models specifically for these target domains. Testing across biomedical and computer science corpora indicates that the proposed method outperforms the BERT BASE architecture in domain-centric benchmarks, while simultaneously achieving 3.3x reduction in size and 5.1x increase in inference speed relative to BERT BASE. Implementation assets and model checkpoints are accessible via https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Applying Teacher-Student Learning to Compact Highway Networks
abstract: Speech recognition performance has improved substantially through recent deep learning innovations. Yet, neural networks often exceed the memory constraints required for mobile hardware deployment when contrasted with traditional Gaussian mixture models. Earlier research explored depth-gated feedforward architectures, specifically highway deep neural networks (HDNN), for acoustic tasks. Those studies demonstrated that HDNN frameworks yield recognition precision similar to standard deep neural networks (DNN) while utilizing fewer total model parameters. This article extends that work by implementing teacher-student distillation, where a high-performance, complex model guides the training of a lightweight HDNN. Additionally, the study evaluates how sequence-level optimization and adaptation integrate with teacher-student methods. Testing on the AMI meeting corpus revealed that this approach markedly enhances the recognition capabilities of an HDNN with a sub-0.8 million parameter footprint, effectively bridging the performance divide between it and a 30 million parameter plain DNN.
